reviews.text: This is a perfect game if you need to brush up on your basic math functions, and it is fun to pass the time. One thing that I noticed Is that the achievements do not work, as I have no achievements, but I should have the achievements for getting ten stars, and for beating the first area. Overall, pretty good game for $5.50, and you should give it a try if you like math.

TL;DR Well worth playing, with a few nitpicky flaws here and there. PROS: - Cute artstyle and sound effects. I particularly enjoyed the animations that come with picking up entities and plopping them back down. - The game is generous with undos, so you can experiment without having to slide the calculator out when it comes to three or more digit numbers. Even if you hate doing arithmetic in your head, you can find the solution without doing that with just your general intuition and some clicking around. - Finding out the solution to a boss fight or tricky late round is quite satisfying. - Content feels appropriate for the price. - As of this review, the achievements have been fixed. - The game is satisfying for both adults and children CONS: - Although it's expected that you need to think before acting in turn-based tactics, in my view the flow and pacing of the game is more closely aligned to the puzzle genre, and you can expect to get stuck for a while on some parts. Or maybe I'm just slow lol. In any case, it won't really be like an Advance Wars or Into the Breach kind of feeling if you know what I mean. - Some powers are far more useful than others, such as the one with the rainbow icon that allows you to get away with small remainders in your operations. By useful, I mean the intuitive ease with which you can find a workable solution. - I might be misunderstanding the fundamental game mechanics, but my understanding is that the player is sometimes 'forced' to use their troops in a certain way, for example cloning and sacrifice squirrels to use the two fixed-seed spells that come with them. - I would personally have gone with higher pixel counts on some of the fonts. - The targeting interface is a bit fiddly and it's quite easy to accidentally kill your King by targeting the wrong monster. Ironically, the one move that cannot be undone is the one move that the player will always want to undo! Now that a 'give up' button has been added, I think this would be a straightforward change to make to the game. - In general, I wish there were a smoother way to pair entities for battle and select spells, but I am not sure how the dev would go about it without reworking much of the design, so it's perhaps an unfair expectation. OTHER: I would personally recommend checking out some of the dev's other games, such as Shotgun King, even if you didn't enjoy this one specifically.

Great concept, unbalanced and unfun execution. Algebrawl has the same problems as the Shotgun King did - base difficulty is okay, but the advanced modifiers turn the game into a tedious lock-picking experience, as you keep mashing different numbers together in hopes that they fit the enemy stats. The main problem is that the enemies health is completely random, so the same 4 units can roll different large prime numbers, numbers without a common denominator, and be ~50 HP apart. There's a big difference between fighting a ghost enemy (cannot be hit by a number larger than its health) with 30 health and a ghost with 29 health, for example. Sometimes it's straight up impossible to come up with a clear solution for the level, as your tools are rather scarce. You only gain one spell/unit/perk per treasure and at the latter levels you usually lack one of those to make it through. Your king doesn't regain health and most of the times he's is forced to take a hit, as your units cannot fight a 1HP enemy without corrupting themselves. The Moral perk should be a basekit mechanic btw QoL changes may switch this review into a positive, but as of now this game is just extremely annoying to play

I really can't recommend this game. It is frustratingly easy and hard at the same time. Easy because if you cheese the mechanics of the game (which the game is absolutely encouraging you to do) it becomes a snore-fest of copying, breaking apart, attacking, get spells, repeat. Its hard because it is nearly impossible if you don't use these boring and broken mechanics. The idea of the game is alright. Use math to overcome your enemies, adding units together, splitting them into two halves, multiplying them by themselves. Such and such. Different units have powers, There is a squirrel that when it dies give you a spell, there is a unit that can be broken down to its individual digits, units that can multiply themselves by 2, such and such. My problem with this game lies in these units. Each time you multiply the units with powers with other units, they get to keep their powers. So if you multiply the Squirrel with the one that can break itself into pieces, you end up with a unit that can break itself up into different pieces that all give a spell. With nothing but at least one split or clone and, and either a multiplier or an addition spell. You have an infinite combo that breaks the game. You get that Digit breaking squirrel dude to 3 digits, you copy it, you multiply the clone with the original (now each unit gives 2 spells on death) you break it apart to usually 4-5 units by now, so 10 spells. In those 10 spells the likelihood that you aren't gonna get a split or a clone is super narrow. But if you don't, you just take the last one and you multiply him or add as many as you can, because he can STILL break into more digits (and that works for each time you multiply the same power into itself.) With this combo, I finish the last difficulty in one try. After spending so long trying to actually play this game and running into wall after wall because I didn't pick the right tools for the job, it is very frustrating to have no threats left in the game. Cute idea for a game, but overall I think it is just a letdown at the end.

I think this game is neat in principle but I think the overall design is kind of flawed. To my understanding, the game will generate puzzles that are somehow possible with your current troops/items. If this is wrong, please let me know because that would invalidate this entire review, but I'm going with that assumption since I feel like it's true from experience. With that said, you really aren't incentivized to get anything "good". If whatever you'll be up against will always be *technically* possible to beat with good enough math, why not just get whatever will give you a simple solution? Again, please let me know if I'm wrong about the "enemies are always possible" thing, since this feels like a pretty major design oversight. But if that really is how the game works, there's not much sauce to it as a game rather than just a self-imposed puzzle with a shiny coat of paint, imo. Also, I will say that the art and music design are both pretty great. I think the low resolution gets a bit cramped at times, especially with text, but that's not really an issue outside of the title screen.
外因有点重, 尤其是发牌是有阶段的, 一个阶段里不可能出现下一个阶段甚至是上一个阶段的牌, 这就导致敌人的强度其实是失衡的, 在敌人强度大幅上升之前, 玩家只有大概50%的概率拿到能够将自己的强度提到和敌人持平的状态. 剩下50%就是不发牌被人数值碾压, 甚至浑身解数都达不到敌人一半的数值

You get to play as GANON conquering lands using the TRIFORCE OF MATH It's simple, but quite well done. I don't think you need to be particularly smart to play this, the algebra is within anyone's reach and there's an undo button if you screw up your calculations. The highest numbers I had to deal with were around 4000, and those are just bosses. The fun thing is that you can't just make huge numbers and call it a day - if you kill an enemy using a stronger soldier, this soldier becomes your new enemy (unless you have a certain perk). So you have to be exact. The overall quality of the game is what I've come to expect from PUNKCAKE. There's some weirdness, but it's the good kind of weirdness, and the design is thought out, but not particularly deep. Which is fine! As much as I enjoy some math every now and then, I have plenty of other things to think about... If you like occasionally crunching numbers, then cmon. You have nothing to lose here. Super Algebrawl, developed and published by PUNKCAKE Délicieux, is a clever indie experiment that manages to turn basic algebra into the foundation of a tactical, roguelike-inspired experience. On the surface, it presents itself like a lighthearted pixel-art strategy game, but beneath that playful exterior lies a system where numbers, operations, and logic take the place of traditional combat mechanics. Instead of relying on attacks and damage values, the game asks players to think mathematically, transforming each encounter into a puzzle where success depends on how well you manipulate values to match or overcome your opponents. The core gameplay revolves around controlling units that each carry a numerical value. Enemies also present values, and your goal is to use operations—such as addition, multiplication, duplication, or division—to adjust your numbers until they align with or surpass those of your targets. This creates a loop that feels less like fighting and more like solving equations under pressure. Despite the abstract nature of the system, the game does an excellent job of making it intuitive. Early encounters are simple and easy to understand, allowing players to grasp the basics quickly, while later challenges introduce more complex combinations that require careful planning and creative thinking. What makes Super Algebrawl particularly engaging is how it builds layers of strategy on top of these simple mechanics. As you progress through a run, you gain access to new abilities and modifiers that expand the ways you can manipulate numbers. This opens up multiple possible solutions to each encounter, encouraging experimentation rather than forcing a single correct approach. Some strategies focus on efficiency, reaching the required values in as few steps as possible, while others prioritize safety, minimizing risk even if it takes longer. This flexibility gives the game a depth that goes beyond its initial simplicity, rewarding players who take the time to understand its systems. The roguelike structure adds another dimension to the experience. Each run presents a different set of tools, forcing players to adapt their strategies based on what they are given. This unpredictability keeps the gameplay fresh, as no two runs unfold in exactly the same way. At the same time, it introduces a level of risk, as poor decisions or unlucky combinations can lead to situations that are difficult to recover from. This balance between control and randomness creates a satisfying tension, where planning ahead is just as important as reacting to the current situation. Pacing is one of the game’s strengths. Runs are relatively short, making it easy to jump in for a quick session without committing a large amount of time. This structure complements the puzzle-based gameplay, as it keeps the experience focused and prevents it from becoming overly repetitive. However, this also highlights one of the game’s main limitations: its overall scope is quite small. While the core mechanics are strong, the amount of content is limited, and players will likely encounter most of what the game has to offer within a few hours. This can make the experience feel somewhat brief, especially for those who become invested in its systems. Visually, Super Algebrawl carries a vibrant and expressive pixel-art style that adds personality to its abstract mechanics. Characters and environments are colorful and animated with a playful energy, helping to make the concept of “math combat” feel approachable and fun rather than intimidating. The interface is well-designed, presenting numerical information clearly while still feeling tactile and interactive. This clarity is crucial, as it allows players to focus on solving problems without being hindered by confusing presentation. The audio design complements the game’s tone, providing a lively and upbeat backdrop that matches its quirky aesthetic. While the soundtrack may not be particularly memorable on its own, it supports the overall experience effectively, maintaining a sense of momentum and engagement throughout each run. Despite its strengths, the game does have a few rough edges. As encounters become more complex, the amount of information on screen can occasionally feel overwhelming, making it harder to track all the variables at play. Additionally, while the central mechanic is inventive, it is not expanded upon as much as it could be, leading to a sense that the game’s potential is only partially realized. These issues don’t detract significantly from the experience, but they do limit its long-term appeal. Ultimately, Super Algebrawl succeeds by committing fully to its unique concept and executing it with clarity and creativity. It transforms a subject that is often seen as dry or intimidating into something playful and engaging, offering a fresh take on both puzzle and strategy genres. While its limited content and scope prevent it from feeling like a fully expansive experience, what it does offer is polished, inventive, and consistently enjoyable. In the end, Super Algebrawl stands out as a smart and imaginative indie title that proves how even the simplest ideas—when approached creatively—can lead to something memorable. It may not last long, but it leaves a strong impression through its originality and thoughtful design. Rating: 7/10
